title: Check whether a paper's citations really say what they are cited for, with K2 Horizon
summary: Give K2 Horizon the sentences where a paper cites a reference plus the full text of the cited paper, and get back a verdict (supported / incorrect / unverifiable) with a verbatim quote. A short script then checks that the quote really exists, so you review one passage per reference instead of reading every cited paper. On FastUMI (arXiv 2409.19499) this found 6 mis-cited references out of 21; K2's own verdict was right 17 times out of 21, so a human still makes the final call.
workflow:
Model: IFM/K2-Horizon-375B-A23B through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint https://api.ifm.ai/v1/chat/completions. Python standard library only, plus pdftotext (poppler) for PDFs. Keep the API key in an environment variable, never in the script.

Setup
1. Get the citing paper as text. For arXiv papers, download the HTML version (https://arxiv.org/html/<id>), strip the tags and split it at the last "References" heading into body text and reference list.
2. List the references that carry an arXiv ID ({number: arXiv ID}). For FastUMI that is 21 of 51.
3. For each one, download https://arxiv.org/pdf/<id> and convert it with: pdftotext paper.pdf paper.txt

Steps per reference n
1. Find the citing sentences: split the body into sentences and keep those with a bracket that contains n. Expand ranges, so that [3, 8-10] counts for 3, 8, 9 and 10.
2. Call K2 with response_format {"type": "json_object"}, max_tokens 16000, and chat_template_kwargs {"reasoning_effort": "medium"}. Prompt (shortened):
   "You are auditing a citation in <paper>. It cites reference [n] in these sentences: <sentences>. Reference entry [n]: <entry>. Below is the full text of the cited paper. Decide whether the cited paper supports what the paper uses it for. Return ONLY a JSON object: {"claim": what the paper relies on [n] for, in one sentence; "status": "supported" | "incorrect" | "unverifiable"; "quote": verbatim passage from the CITED paper, max 60 words, "" if unverifiable; "reason": why}. Rules: supported = the cited paper clearly backs the claim; incorrect = it contradicts it or is about something else; unverifiable = the text does not settle it. Copy the quote exactly." Then append the cited paper's text, cut at 150,000 characters.
3. Parse robustly. K2 often writes its reasoning into the content field before the JSON, even in JSON mode. Search for the last occurrence of {"claim" and decode from there with json.JSONDecoder().raw_decode.
4. Retry on failure. If there is no complete JSON (the reply was cut off at max_tokens), save the failed call and run the same prompt again with reasoning_effort "low".
5. Check the quote. Lower-case both texts, undo line-break hyphenation, remove everything except letters and digits, and test whether the quote is a substring of the cited text. Require at least 20 characters so that a quote of "..." cannot pass.
6. Log everything per reference as JSON: citing sentences, prompt size, K2's reasoning and answer, token usage, latency, quote check.

Human check (do not skip)
7. For every reference, read K2's quote in the cited paper and decide the final status yourself. Write down every case where you overrule K2 and why.

Cost: 21 references needed 26 calls including retries and used 679K tokens in total. Most of that is the cited papers' full text in the prompts.
exampleInput:
Citing paper: FastUMI (arXiv 2409.19499). Reference [8]: Chen et al., "ARCap: Collecting high-quality human demonstrations for robot learning with augmented reality feedback", arXiv 2410.08464.

Citing sentences found by the script:
- "Various control interfaces, including AR controllers [31, 8], haptic controllers [29, 13], 3D spacemouses [27], and newly explored leader-follower systems [42] are developed to build teleoperated systems."
- "Furthermore, in dexterous hand manipulation tasks, IL has been extended to learn from human hand motion demonstrations [41, 8]."

Cited paper text: pdftotext of https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.08464 (35,029 characters).

Second example: reference [26] (Levine et al., arXiv 1603.02199), cited in "Current methods can be broadly categorized into teleoperation-based techniques [...], vision-driven demonstrations [3, 26], and sensor-enhanced interfaces [...]."
checkedOutput:
Reference [8]: K2 returned the following (10,798 tokens, quote found verbatim in the cited text):
status: incorrect
quote: "We propose ARCap, a portable data collection system that provides visual feedback through augmented reality (AR) and haptic warnings to guide users in collecting high-quality demonstrations."
reason: ARCap is a portable data collection system without robot hardware, not a teleoperation control interface, so the first use is incorrect; the second use (IL from human hand motion demonstrations) is supported.
My check: I agree. I read the quoted passage and the ARCap introduction. It is an AR data-collection system, not an AR controller for teleoperation. The second use is fine.

Reference [26]: K2 returned "supported", with the real quote "We describe a learning-based approach to hand-eye coordination for robotic grasping from monocular images."
My check: I overruled K2 and marked it incorrect. FastUMI lists [26] as a "vision-driven demonstration" method, but the cited paper learns from the robots' own 800,000 grasp attempts ("we collected over 800,000 grasp attempts ... using between 6 and 14 robotic manipulators") and uses no demonstrations at all. The quote K2 picked was true but did not address the actual claim.

Whole run (21 references): 15 supported and 6 incorrect after review. K2's status was wrong 4 times: [14] and [43] were too strict, [26] and [40] too lenient. 20 of 21 quotes passed the automatic check. The one that failed ([3]) is real; pdftotext had split it with a figure caption.
limitations:
- K2's verdict is a first pass, not an answer. It was wrong on about 1 in 5 references here, in both directions. A real quote that is true but beside the point (as in [26]) is the typical failure, so always check that the quote addresses the specific claim.
- It needs the cited paper's full text. In this run only references with an arXiv ID were covered (21 of 51); books, journal-only papers and web pages still have to be checked by hand.
- Long cited papers are cut at 150,000 characters. Here that affected one review paper of 205K characters, so evidence near its end could be missed.
- K2 sometimes puts its reasoning inside the answer, spends the whole token budget on reasoning (4 of 26 calls were cut off at 16K tokens), or returns a placeholder quote such as "...". The parser, the low-effort retry and the 20-character quote check handle these cases; keep the failed calls in your logs.
- pdftotext layout noise (captions, two-column breaks) can make a real quote fail the automatic check, so look up failed quotes by hand before calling them fabricated.
- "Supported" here means only that the cited paper says it. It does not mean the claim itself is true.
